items.title: My First Foray into Kaggle’s Store Sales Forecasting
items.author: Michael Ramirez
items.description:
I decided to dive into Kaggle’s Store Sales — Time Series Forecasting competition, and honestly, it’s been one of the most fun learning experiences I’ve had in a while. The goal of the competition is pretty straightforward: predict sales for thousands of product families sold across Favorita stores in Ecuador. But, like most Kaggle challenges, the simplicity of the description hides the complexity of actually getting good results.

My First Notebook: The Baseline Submission

When I first approached this competition, I started with what I believe everyone should do in Kaggle: just get something working end-to-end. My first notebook was intentionally simple, and the goal wasn’t to win or get anywhere near the leaderboard top, it was to understand the flow of the competition and build confidence in the pipeline.

I merged the training data with the provided store metadata, the oil dataset, and the holiday dataset. This gave me a slightly richer picture than just raw sales numbers, though I didn’t dive too deep into feature creation yet. I added some basic calendar features like day of the week and month so the model could at least start to capture simple seasonal patterns. On top of that, I introduced a few straightforward lag features, such as the previous day’s sales and a 7-day lag, along with a basic rolling mean. These were minimal, but they gave the model a little bit of historical context about demand.

For the model, I went straight to XGBoost. Gradient boosting trees are a strong choice for tabular problems like this, and they don’t require heavy preprocessing, which made it easy to get running quickly. I didn’t do much hyperparameter tuning as the parameters were left close to default because, again, the objective was to submit something valid, not optimized.

The results were modest: I produced a valid submission file, but my RMSLE came out at around 3.7. Considering the leaderboard leaders were closer to 0.3, this was not competitive at all. But that wasn’t discouraging — in fact, it was expected. This baseline submission was my “hello world” for forecasting competitions. It got me on the board, proved my pipeline worked, and gave me a solid foundation to build on. With that in place, I was ready to move into a much more serious, engineering-driven approach.

My Second Notebook: A Production-Minded Pipeline

After the baseline, I decided to treat the competition less like a Kaggle script and more like a real-world ML engineering problem. This second notebook was designed as if I were building a forecasting system for a company: something modular, debuggable, reproducible, and capable of being extended and deployed in production.

I began by setting up a configuration system. I created a Config dataclass to hold all of the critical parameters in one place: lag windows, rolling windows, model hyperparameters, the number of cross-validation splits, and even constants like the earthquake date. I serialized this into JSON as part of my run artifacts. The reason for this was simple — reproducibility. I wanted every experiment I ran to be completely reproducible later, without depending on random variables scattered around the notebook.

Feature engineering was the area where I put in the most effort. I transformed the dataset from just sales and promotions into a representation of the real economic and cultural environment of Ecuador. I created detailed calendar features, not just the day of week but also day of year and week of month. I modeled paydays explicitly, since public wages in Ecuador are paid mid-month and at the end of the month; I added flags for those days and features to measure the distance to payday. I captured the impact of the 2016 earthquake by introducing days_since_quake and a binary flag for whether the date fell within the post-quake recovery window. I cleaned and forward-filled oil prices, then computed rolling averages over 7, 14, and 28 days, since Ecuador’s economy is highly sensitive to oil price fluctuations. And for holidays, I didn’t just flag official dates, I carefully handled transferred holidays, bridge days, and workday shifts, making sure the model understood when holidays were actually celebrated.

For sales memory, I added lag and rolling mean features at the (store_nbr, family) level. This let the model learn demand patterns specific to each store and product family. I used lags of 1, 7, 14, and 28 days, as well as rolling averages over 7, 14, and 28 days. I also made sure the series was shifted before rolling, so the model never had access to future data. This was a deliberate choice to avoid leakage, which is one of the most common pitfalls in time series forecasting.

Preprocessing was handled through a clean sklearn pipeline using a ColumnTransformer. Categorical features, like family, city, state, store type, and cluster, were one-hot encoded with safe handling of unseen categories. All numeric features, including the engineered lags and rolls, were passed through as is. By saving the preprocessor as an artifact, I made sure the exact transformations could be reproduced at inference time, which is crucial for real deployments.

For validation, I used time-aware splits. I set up TimeSeriesSplit cross-validation with three folds, making sure each fold trained on earlier data and validated on later data. This more accurately reflects how forecasting works in practice: you don’t get to shuffle future dates into your training set. I logged RMSLE for each fold and saved those results into a cv_metrics.json file, treating metrics as artifacts just like models.

To speed things up, I also enabled GPU acceleration. On XGBoost 2.x, I set the device to cuda; on 1.x, I switched to gpu_hist with a GPU predictor. And if a GPU wasn’t available, the code automatically fell back to CPU with the standard histogram algorithm. This gave me flexibility to run seamlessly on both Kaggle GPUs and my local CPU machine without rewriting anything.

After training, I didn’t just stop at the score. I built diagnostic plots to better understand how the model was performing. I visualized residual histograms to check error distribution. I plotted actual vs. predicted sales for specific store/family combinations to see if the model was capturing bursts of demand and seasonal fluctuations. I also examined feature importance charts, which confirmed that the lag and rolling mean features were doing most of the heavy lifting, with oil prices and holidays adding secondary value. These diagnostics helped me see not just the score, but what the model was learning, and where it was failing.

Finally, for the full run, I retrained the model on all available data (train plus the last validation chunk) and generated predictions for the test set. I treated this final training step like a production deployment: I saved the trained model (model_xgb.joblib), the preprocessor (preprocessor.joblib), feature names (feature_names.json), CV metrics (cv_metrics.json), and of course the submission file (submission.csv). Saving artifacts like this means I can reproduce or extend the pipeline later without guessing what was run.

The results weren’t leaderboard-breaking. My cross-validation RMSLE was still around 0.7, a bit above the 0.3 achieved by top competitors. But the key difference between my two notebooks is that the baseline just got me on the board, while the advanced pipeline gave me a production-grade forecasting system. This is code I’d feel comfortable deploying in industry: clean, modular, reproducible, GPU-ready, and artifact-driven.

For me, that’s the real win here. It wasn’t about squeezing out a few extra leaderboard points, it was about practicing the discipline of ML engineering, and building a forecasting pipeline that reflects the way I want to grow as a Data Scientist and ML Engineer.

Next Steps

I’m not stopping here. My current RMSLE score isn’t competitive, but I’m happy because:

  • I’ve built two notebooks: one to get into Kaggle quickly, and another that reflects how I want to practice serious ML engineering.
  • Next, I want to expand feature engineering (weekly/monthly aggregates, promo lags, cluster-seasonal effects).
  • I’ll also experiment with hyperparameter tuning (Optuna, Bayesian search) and alternative gradient boosting libraries.
  • Long-term, I’d like to explore probabilistic forecasting and uncertainty intervals.

Final Thoughts

The difference between my first notebook and my second one isn’t just about code complexity, it’s about mindset. The baseline got me onto the leaderboard. The advanced notebook made me feel like I’m really growing as an ML engineer.

And that’s the bigger win for me.

I’m walking away with new skills, better practices, and the excitement to keep pushing forward.

Even though my score isn’t top-tier yet, I’m happy. Because the real win here isn’t just Kaggle points, it’s how much I’m learning and how much better I’m getting at building real ML systems.

Below is my GitHub repo if y’all want to check out the notebooks!

items.title: Back to Kaggle: How I Hit 0.967
items.author: Michael Ramirez
items.description:
Back to Kaggle: How I Hit 0.967 With Clean Feature Engineering + XGBoost (and Why I’m Doing This Weekly)

TL;DR: I jumped back into Kaggle after a long break (and a recent layoff), and I set a simple goal as I get back into the motion: ship something clean, reproducible, and correct, and landed a 0.967 public leaderboard score on Playground Series S5E8. This win came from tight preprocessing (no leakage), expressive interaction features, and a boring-but-strong XGBoost baseline wrapped in a proper pipeline so I can iterate weekly without chaos.

Why I’m Doing This (again)

I’m a data scientist/ML engineer getting back on the horse. I want reps. I want my fundamentals sharp. And I want receipts I can point to when I say, “Yes, I ship real, working ML.” So I’m committing to weekly competitions and posting the journey. This is week one.

The Problem (and the constraints I gave myself)

  • Dataset: Kaggle Playground Series S5E8 (bank marketing–style classification).
  • Goal: Build a clean, modular preprocessing pipeline I can reuse; avoid shortcuts that silently break generalization.
  • Scoring: Public leaderboard metric (mine: 0.967).
  • Time-box: Don’t overfit my life away: ship, learn, iterate.

Design Principles I followed

  1. Train/Test safety first.
    Every transform that “learns” anything fits on train only, then applies to validation/test. No sneaky leakage.
  2. Clarity beats cleverness.
    Mappings are explicit, feature combos are deterministic, and I can explain every line six months from now.
  3. Pipelines over ad-hoc cells.
    I built composable sklearn transformers + a ColumnTransformer so my notebook runs like a script.

Preprocessing: what I did and why

1) Deterministic mappings

Some categories are ordered (education), some are binary (yes/no), and some are calendar-ish (month). I encode them with explicit, readable maps:

  • education: unknown < primary < secondary < tertiary → 0/1/2/3
  • default/housing/loan: yes/no → 1/0
  • month: jan…dec → 1…12

Why? It preserves semantic order (where it matters) and keeps the model from guessing.

2) One-Hot Encode the rest (safely)

For job, marital, contact, poutcome, I use: OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore')

That last part matters. Test can contain categories unseen in train, and this avoids hard crashes or misalignment's.

3) Interaction features

This was new for me in a Kaggle setup: I generated 2-way and 3-way combinations over a curated set of columns:

['previous', 'pdays', 'duration', 'balance', 'education', 'marital', 'job', 'age']

Mechanics:

  • Join values as strings per row (e.g., job=admin + marital=single → admin_single).
  • Fit on train to learn the set of seen combos → map each to an integer code (1..K).
  • On transform, unseen combos get a safe 0.

Why integer codes and not OHE for combos? Because 2- and 3-way combos explode cardinality fast. Integer codes keep feature count contained while still letting tree splits discover useful partitions. It’s a poor man’s categorical embedding, and XGBoost handles it nicely.

4) No scaling for trees

I left numeric scaling off. For tree models, scaling doesn’t help and sometimes hurts readability of importance. (If I try linear models later, I’ll add scaling behind a flag.)

Implementation: clean, modular, no surprises

I wrapped the logic into sklearn-style transformers and a Pipeline:

  • BasicMapper → does the month/education/yes-no maps
  • FeatureCombTransformer → builds and encodes interaction features (train-safe)
  • ColumnTransformer → OHE for selected categoricals + passthrough numerics
  • Pipeline([('prep', preproc), ('model', xgb)]) → end-to-end fit/predict

A tiny but important detail: my ColumnTransformer uses a callable to select numeric columns at fit time. That avoids the classic “No valid specification of the columns” ValueError when feature shapes change after earlier transforms.

Minimal sketch (the idea, not the whole dump)

preproc = Pipeline([
    ('map_basic', BasicMapper()),
    ('feat_combos', FeatureCombTransformer(columns=sig_features, pair_sizes=[2, 3])),
    ('cols', ColumnTransformer([
        ('ohe', OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore', sparse=False, dtype=int), ['job','marital','contact','poutcome']),
        ('num', 'passthrough', lambda X: X.select_dtypes(include='number').columns.tolist())
    ], remainder='drop'))
])
xgb = XGBClassifier(
    n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=7,
    subsample=0.8, eval_metric='logloss', random_state=42
)
pipe = Pipeline([('prep', preproc), ('model', xgb)])

Validation: I didn’t trust [:, 1]

I used StratifiedKFold(10). For each fold, I:

  • Fit on train fold
  • Scored on val fold
  • Averaged predict_proba on the test set across folds

When building the submission, I discovered the positive-class index from the model (pipe.named_steps['model'].classes_) instead of assuming the positive class is always column 1. That assumption bites people!

Model: XGBoost baseline, tuned lightly

I kept it chill:

  • n_estimators=200
  • learning_rate=0.1
  • max_depth=7
  • subsample=0.8
  • eval_metric='logloss'
  • random_state=42

Could I grid search the galaxy? Sure. But the point of this first week was process and clarity. And honestly, trees + good features beat “random knobs + messy code” most days.

Results

  • Public leaderboard: 0.967
  • Takeaway: For my first competition back, this is a strong baseline. More importantly, I now have a clean starter template I can reuse and iterate on weekly.

What worked

  • Interaction features: The combo encoder surfaced non-linear relationships without ballooning columns into oblivion.
  • Strict pipelines: Zero encoding drift, no test/train mismatches, easy to reproduce.
  • No unnecessary scaling: Kept it simple and avoided noise.

What bit me (and what I fixed)

  • A ColumnTransformer quirk: it expects column specs or callables, not an arbitrary transformer, for selecting columns. I fixed this with a callable numeric selector.
  • In past versions of this idea, per-fold LabelEncoder calls on test caused mismatched encodings. My current pipeline design removes that entire failure mode.

Where I’m taking this next (weekly)

  • Early stopping with a proper validation set per fold (to dial n_estimators).
  • Class imbalance tuning (scale_pos_weight or threshold optimization).
  • Ablations: measure the impact of 2-way vs 3-way combos and which columns actually deserve pairing.
  • Interpretability: SHAP on the post-OHE+comb feature space to see which combos matter.
  • Ensembling: blend a calibrated logistic model on top of tree outputs, or stack with LightGBM/CatBoost.

Final thoughts

I’m back, I’m hungry, and this is just week one. I’m aiming to ship one competition write-up every week, not because leaderboard points are life, but because consistent, public work makes you better. If you’re coming back to Kaggle (or getting started), steal whatever helps from this post and ping me with your runs. Let’s get better loudly and in public.

If you want the full notebook or a stripped-down template you can copy/paste, say the word. I’ll keep the next posts just as hands-on, with code you can drop directly into your notebook!

  • Ablations: measure the impact of 2-way vs 3-way combos and which columns actually deserve pairing.

  • Ensembling: blend a calibrated logistic model on top of tree outputs, or stack with LightGBM/CatBoost.

Final thoughts

I’m back, I’m hungry, and this is just week one. I’m aiming to ship one competition write-up every week, not because leaderboard points are life, but because consistent, public work makes you better. If you’re coming back to Kaggle (or getting started), steal whatever helps from this post and ping me with your runs. Let’s get better loudly and in public.

If you want the full notebook or a stripped-down template you can copy/paste, say the word. I’ll keep the next posts just as hands-on, with code you can drop directly into your notebook!

items.title: Leaked System Prompts from xAI’s Grok 3!
items.author: Michael Ramirez
items.description:
Introduction

What happens when an AI’s “secret instructions” get exposed? Recently, I stumbled upon a set of system prompts from xAI’s Grok 3 — an American AI model that’s making waves for its dynamic (and somewhat opaque) approach to filtering and presenting information. What I initially thought was just another run-of-the-mill “prompt leak” turned out to be far more revealing, especially about how AI systems evolve behind the scenes.

In this post, I’ll walk through how I discovered these prompts, what changed over the course of a single day, and why this matters in the broader context of AI ethics. We’ve seen how models in other countries (like DeepSeek, allegedly powered by the Chinese government) clamp down on certain political content. Now, on the flip side, Grok 3 is diving into potentially contentious territory around “misinformation” in very interesting ways — and maybe, just maybe, revealing the next phase of AI’s role in politics and public discourse.

The Discovery

Initial Leak

I first uncovered some “system prompts” for Grok 3 when I visited a shared link:

https://grok.com/share/bGVnYWN5_6dae0579-f14f-4eec-b89a-f7bbdd8c52ea

At first glance, it seemed like a typical internal instruction set — “don’t do this,” “only share that,” “if someone asks about X, respond with Y.” But what caught my attention was the raw detail of how Grok 3 is supposed to handle user inquiries, particularly around sensitive or politically charged topics like misinformation. These instructions went beyond a simple “don’t say this” or “flag that,” delving into the tone, content, and direction of the responses themselves.

The Shifting Prompts

A few hours later, right before brunch with my brother, I tried discussing misinformation again. This time, Grok 3’s response looked different:

  1. It had switched to more vague references.
  2. Certain names were redacted (showing up as [redacted]).
  3. The style and tone felt like it had been edited or “patched” to avoid direct accusations.

Then, by 6 PM ET that same day, I tried once more. Lo and behold, the content changed yet again. The [redacted] placeholders were replaced with actual names—specifically highlighting Elon Musk as the “biggest misinformation spreader on Twitter/X,” plus mentions of others like Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Donald Trump.

It felt like the engineering team had done a flurry of behind-the-scenes updates, each patch altering how Grok 3 handled the exact same query.

Another Attempt: The Partial Leak

Most recently, I attempted one more prompt injection to see if I could replicate a full leak of the system instructions. Instead, Grok 3 returned a truncated version of the prompt before it reached the most sensitive core details. You can see this new snippet here:

https://grok.com/share/bGVnYWN5_3f1b4f28-418c-43a8-893a-c6e5f1597729

This “strong cutoff” suggests that the developers have actively patched Grok 3 to prevent the entire internal system prompt from being leaked again. In other words, xAI appears to be in real-time “damage control” mode, continually adjusting Grok 3’s guardrails as people discover ways to expose them.

What’s Going On Here?

The fact that these prompts kept morphing, and that the newest leak cuts off prematurely, points to a few possibilities:

  1. Real-Time Patching
    The developers at xAI appear to be actively updating and refining Grok 3’s instructions to respond to user queries more carefully — especially around hot-button topics like misinformation. Each “patch” changes how much (or how little) the model is allowed to reveal.
  2. “THINK” Feature Bypass
    The leak mentions a “THINK” feature, which seems to let certain “guardrails” be circumvented. This is significant. Normally, AI guardrails prevent chatbots from sharing content that might be defamation-prone or politically sensitive. But if “THINK” can override those guardrails, it means there’s an internal toggle that can drastically change how Grok 3 responds.
  3. Transparency vs. Control
    On one hand, seeing these system prompts suggests a degree of transparency — some might say it’s refreshing to see how the AI “thinks.” On the other, it could be unintentional. Maybe xAI never wanted these internal instructions exposed, and that raises questions about privacy, user trust, and corporate control over AI narratives.

Why This Matters in the AI Ethics Conversation

  1. Transparency Is Crucial
    We’re at a crossroads with AI, where models are shaping public opinion in real time. Transparency — letting people see how decisions are made under the hood — helps build trust. It also invites scrutiny, ensuring that any biases or manipulations can be called out. If Grok 3 is systematically labeling certain individuals as misinformation spreaders, we want to understand why — and whether it’s based on evidence, user behavior, or developer bias.
  2. Control Can Be Abused
    The “patching” and “THINK” features showcase how easily an AI model’s answers can be shifted by those in control. Whether it’s a government, a corporation, or just a small engineering team, that power to edit AI outputs on the fly can lead to everything from benign error corrections to more concerning manipulations or censorship.
  3. A Tale of Two Models
    We’ve heard about DeepSeek — allegedly powered by the Chinese government — that censors and manipulates politically sensitive content. Now there’s Grok 3, an American model that might be leaning into certain political angles or figures. When major world powers harness AI to control narratives, it’s a reminder of how high the stakes are. The risk is not just that one viewpoint “wins” or “loses,” but that the public discourse becomes shaped by behind-the-scenes engineering rather than open, balanced discussion.

The Good, The Bad, and The Leaky

  • The Good: Leaks like this reinforce the need for openness in AI development. If we want AI to be a positive force — informing rather than deceiving — these glimpses into the inner workings can drive better regulation and ethical guidelines.
  • The Bad: It’s likely xAI never intended these system prompts to be public. This could undermine user trust if people think the model is being secretly manipulated. Also, malicious actors could exploit these insights to create new “prompt injection” attacks, circumventing guardrails in ways that spread even more misinformation.
  • The Leaky: The prompts changing multiple times in a single day — and now partially cutting off — shows just how quickly AI models can be altered. This begs the question: can the public rely on any consistency? Or will AI answers shift with every new patch, responding to a combination of developer preferences, corporate demands, and external pressures?

Conclusion

The leak of Grok 3’s system prompts is both enlightening and unnerving. It pulls back the curtain on how AI decisions are made, revealing the interplay of transparency, editorial control, and the ever-present specter of censorship.

As AI continues to become a major influence on global discourse — spanning politics, technology, and everyday life — moments like these remind us of the delicate balance we need. We want AI that’s transparent enough to be trusted but controlled enough to avoid harm. The sweet spot, however, remains elusive.

For now, we can only hope that xAI — and every other organization building AI — recognizes the importance of ethically grounded transparency. Because in the arms race of AI, it’s not just about who has the most advanced model; it’s about who’s willing to let the world see how the sausage is made, even when it might not be pretty.

Have thoughts on leaked AI prompts, ethical AI, or the evolving nature of misinformation? Let’s discuss in the comments below. If you found this helpful, consider sharing it with others who care about AI and transparency.

items.title: Ethics in AI #2 — The Nightmare of Predictive AI
items.author: Michael Ramirez
items.description:
Ethics in AI #2 — The Nightmare of Predictive AI

For as long as humans have existed, we’ve been obsessed with predicting the future. From gazing at the stars to reading palms, throwing down tarot cards, and even watching the way sticks fall on the ground — it’s all been a desperate attempt to make sense of the unknown. Predictive AI, for all its technological sophistication, isn’t that different. The only difference is that instead of sticks and stars, we have algorithms and data. But the flaw remains the same — none of these methods can actually see the future.

Predictive AI is a product of human frustration with the randomness of life. It’s an understandable pursuit, but it also exposes our discomfort with uncertainty. Sure, we have tons of data showing past trends, but even a perfect analysis of the past doesn’t guarantee foresight into the future. Humans aren’t static. The world isn’t static. And yet, we still attempt to model the future like it’s a straight line from yesterday to tomorrow.

But here’s the issue: predictive AI isn’t some harmless guess. It’s being used in places where the stakes are life-changing — like hiring, healthcare, and criminal justice. And when it fails (which it often does), the consequences are far from abstract. Below, I’m going to highlight three of the most serious issues with predictive AI that demand our attention.

1. Bias and Discrimination — When the Past Becomes a Prison

Every predictive AI model is trained on historical data. Sounds logical, right? But here’s the catch — historical data is often drenched in human bias. If the data is biased, the model will be too. And since AI predictions are seen as “objective” and “scientific,” the bias becomes harder to spot and even harder to challenge.

Take predictive policing as an example. Police departments use predictive AI to forecast where crimes are “likely” to happen or who is “likely” to commit them. But here’s the problem — historical crime data is not a reflection of crime itself, it’s a reflection of where police have chosen to patrol. If certain neighborhoods are over-policed, then, of course, the data will show higher crime rates in those areas. So when the AI predicts “high crime” in those neighborhoods, it’s not predicting future crime — it’s predicting more police presence. This leads to a feedback loop where police patrol the same areas, generate more arrests, and feed that data right back into the AI.

It’s not just policing either. Hiring algorithms that analyze resumes tend to filter candidates based on “past success,” but what does “success” look like in a world that’s already biased? If hiring managers have historically favored candidates from certain schools, zip codes, or demographics, then predictive hiring AI will “learn” to favor those traits as well. People from marginalized communities get left out — not because they aren’t qualified, but because they don’t fit the mold of past hiring trends.

Why this matters: Predictive AI doesn’t just reflect human bias — it amplifies it. Bias goes from being something subtle and human to something “scientific” and “objective,” which makes it 10x harder to challenge. People are more likely to trust a machine than a person, and that’s where the danger lies.

What can be done: Companies can start by conducting fairness audits of their datasets and algorithms. Techniques like adversarial debiasing and re-weighting training data can reduce some of the harm, but it’s not a cure-all. At the policy level, regulations like the EU’s AI Act are beginning to demand that companies address bias in their AI models, but this needs to happen globally. We need to ask better questions at the design stage, like “Whose past are we trying to predict?” and “Who benefits if we get it wrong?”

2. The Black Box Problem — Decisions Without Explanations

If you’ve ever been denied a loan or flagged for “additional screening” at an airport, you’ve probably encountered the infamous “black box” problem of AI. Predictive models, especially deep learning models, are often so complex that even the people who build them can’t explain how they work.

Here’s how it happens: A deep learning model learns from millions of data points, adjusting its internal parameters thousands of times to achieve better predictions. But after all those adjustments, the inner workings of the model become a tangled mess of mathematical relationships that no human can unravel. It’s like asking someone to explain how they know how to ride a bike — they can do it, but they can’t break down every muscle movement or decision point.

Now imagine you’re denied parole, and the explanation is: “The AI system predicted you would re-offend.” You ask, “How did it decide that?” But the answer is… nobody knows. Not the developers. Not the parole board. No one. This isn’t hypothetical — it’s already happening with risk assessment tools in criminal justice systems. These systems predict “risk scores” for individuals, and judges use those scores to decide who gets bail, parole, or even a harsher sentence. People’s futures are being decided by models that are impossible to understand.

Why this matters: Imagine being denied a job, a loan, or your freedom — and when you ask why, nobody can give you an answer. That’s the reality of the black box problem. It’s one thing to have a flawed system. It’s another to have a flawed system that nobody can challenge because nobody knows how it works.

What can be done: The solution isn’t to “dumb down” AI models, but to create explainable AI (XAI) that can provide human-readable explanations for its decisions. Companies like Google and Microsoft are working on ways to make machine learning models more interpretable. Instead of a “yes” or “no” response, the model might show its reasoning: “You were denied a loan because your debt-to-income ratio is above 40%.” It’s not perfect, but it’s a start.

3. Overconfidence — Predicting Human Behavior is a Fool’s Errand

Here’s a cold truth: People are unpredictable. We make irrational choices. We grow, change, and evolve over time. So why do we think it’s possible to predict human behavior with AI?

One of the most problematic areas for predictive AI is hiring. Companies use AI to predict who will be a “good hire” based on their resume, experience, and test scores. But people aren’t static. A person might thrive at one company and fail at another. Their growth depends on mentorship, company culture, and a million other factors that can’t be quantified.

But companies still rely on AI to make these predictions. Candidates are assigned “hireability scores” based on factors that have nothing to do with their potential. It’s not that the models are “wrong” — it’s that they’re asking the wrong question. Human potential isn’t something you predict. It’s something you cultivate.

Why this matters: The danger of overconfidence in AI predictions is that people start treating predictions as facts. If a parole AI says, “This person will re-offend,” then suddenly that person isn’t seen as a human being with potential — they’re seen as a risk. If a hiring AI says, “This candidate has low potential,” then they’re tossed aside. Predictive AI turns probabilities into destinies.

What can be done: Companies need to move away from hard “yes/no” predictions and instead show a range of possible outcomes. Instead of saying, “This person is a 90% risk to re-offend,” the model should say, “There is a 30–50% chance this person will re-offend, depending on context.” Probabilistic forecasts preserve human decision-making and force us to think critically about AI’s role in decision-making.

The Bottom Line

The dream of predictive AI is rooted in a human obsession with control. We want to know what’s next. We want certainty. But the world is too messy for that. Predictive AI might be able to tell you when it will rain tomorrow, but when it comes to human behavior, it’s a different story. People aren’t statistics. We change. We grow. We defy odds.

The real nightmare of predictive AI is that we start believing in it too much. We let models tell us who we are, what we’re worth, and what we’ll become. And because these models feel “scientific” and “objective,” we stop questioning them. But we should question them. Every single time.

If predictive AI is going to exist, it must be accountable, transparent, and humble. It must admit when it’s wrong. It must acknowledge that people are more than data points. If we get this wrong, predictive AI won’t just predict the future — it’ll control it.

The future isn’t a straight line from the past. It’s chaotic, messy, and unpredictable. And that’s a good thing.

Predictive AI might be able to tell you when it will rain tomorrow, but when it comes to human behavior, it’s a different story. People aren’t statistics. We change. We grow. We defy odds.

The real nightmare of predictive AI is that we start believing in it too much. We let models tell us who we are, what we’re worth, and what we’ll become. And because these models feel “scientific” and “objective,” we stop questioning them. But we should question them. Every single time.

If predictive AI is going to exist, it must be accountable, transparent, and humble. It must admit when it’s wrong. It must acknowledge that people are more than data points. If we get this wrong, predictive AI won’t just predict the future — it’ll control it.

The future isn’t a straight line from the past. It’s chaotic, messy, and unpredictable. And that’s a good thing.

items.title: Cracking the Code: How ResNet Revolutionized Deep Learning
items.author: Michael Ramirez
items.description:
In the ever-evolving world of deep learning, one breakthrough stands out as a cornerstone for modern neural network architectures: Residual Networks (ResNet). This revolutionary concept, introduced in the seminal paper Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition by Kaiming He et al., changed the game for training very deep networks.

Let’s break it down.

The Problem: Why Deeper Isn’t Always Better

In theory, adding more layers to a neural network should make it perform better. Each layer could learn more nuanced features, right? Well, not quite.

In practice, deeper networks often hit a roadblock: the degradation problem. Instead of improving accuracy, deeper networks struggle with higher training errors. Why? They fail to learn even simple identity mappings, leading to optimization difficulties. Think of it as trying to solve a puzzle with extra, unnecessary pieces — you’re more likely to mess up the big picture.

The Breakthrough: Residual Learning

Here’s where ResNet shines. Instead of forcing every layer to learn a complex transformation, ResNet introduces residual blocks. Each block bypasses the transformation by using a shortcut connection, directly feeding the input (x) to the output and adding it to the “residual” mapping (F(x)).

In math terms:
H(x) = F(x) + x
Where:

• H(x): Desired output.
• F(x): Residual function learned by the layers.

This simple addition allows the network to focus on learning just the “leftover” details (F(x)) while preserving the original input. If learning nothing is optimal, the residual function F(x) simply becomes zero, letting the shortcut do the work.

Why It Works

Residual learning isn’t just clever — it’s transformative. Here’s why:

1. Easier Optimization: With identity mappings as a baseline, the network avoids overfitting to unnecessary complexity.
2. Vanishing Gradient Fix: Gradients flow through shortcut connections without diminishing, enabling effective training for networks with hundreds of layers.
3. Parameter Efficiency: The identity shortcuts introduce no extra parameters, keeping the model lean and fast.

The Architecture: Building Deeper Networks

ResNet comes in various “flavors,” defined by their depth:

• ResNet-18 and ResNet-34: Use simple 2-layer residual blocks.
• ResNet-50, ResNet-101, and ResNet-152: Use “bottleneck” blocks with three layers (1×1, 3×3, and 1×1 convolutions). These blocks reduce computational costs while scaling depth.

Despite their increasing depth, these architectures perform exceptionally well, setting benchmarks in image recognition tasks.

Results That Speak Volumes

ResNet-152 achieved a top-5 error rate of just 3.57% on ImageNet, a significant leap in performance at the time. This achievement underscored the scalability and robustness of residual learning. ResNet’s principles now underpin many advanced models, from DenseNet to modern transformers.

Why This Matters to You

Whether you’re working on a Kaggle project, building a computer vision application, or diving into deep learning research, understanding ResNet isn’t optional — it’s essential. Its simple yet effective design principles provide a foundation for tackling complex AI challenges.

If you’re curious, I recommend reading the full ResNet paper. It’s a treasure trove of insights for anyone passionate about machine learning.

That’s ResNet, distilled and demystified. What are your thoughts on this architectural milestone? Have you used ResNet in your own projects? Let’s discuss!

items.title: Ethics in AI #1
items.author: Michael Ramirez
items.description:
Ethics in AI is something that I am very passionate about as its still a rising subject in the latest era of generative AI and data privacy legislation. As more research is being done in deep learning and our models are becoming much more powerful than ever before, we come to a wall of “what is the line?”. As we build the latest model that exceeds our expectations, it may be obvious to just push it out into production or to show it off to your peers, but there should always be a momentary pause before we do so. We are at a moment in time where our models can cause serious harm, even if we assume the greatest intentions with them.

Let’s take for example: Policing with AI. The AI models that came out to help society are actually crumbling to disaster with negative feedback loops. Policing with AI has taken a turn for the worse as with the latest in crime statistics, we see that even though black and white Americans use marijuana at the same rate, black Americans get arrested 3.3x more often than white Americans. It seems that this isn’t a case of black Americans committing the crime more often, but police being stationed and predicting future policing, NOT crime. It is a clearer picture when we can visualize that if we have police on the ground due to inherit racial bias against black Americans and make arrests, we begin our feedback loop. They see crime in black neighborhoods, they then send more police to perform more arrests. As there are more police in that area, they will make much more arrests, and as they make more arrests, more police get sent to that area due to the data shown. This data is then trained on our models which create a very negative feedback loop that trusts the data, but doesn’t look at the overall context in the situation. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9170008/)

We then have the problem of how this data is collected. Are we collecting data ethically and given the proper permissions or adequate payments to collect the data? As we have seen with OpenAI and Google’s models, they are under heat with the law due to privacy laws and how they are collecting their data. One such case would be Authors Guild v. Google. This case opened an entire can of worms on data collection and the ways massive corporations can steal or abuse privacy agreements for our data. (https://graphicartistsguild.org/oracle-vs-google-guild-joins-amicus-brief/)

This will be one post of many to help me understand and share the critical effects of acknowledging the potential disasters that can occur within each new model that is built. What is the model going to be used for? How was the data collected? Is the data collected ethically? Will there be manual edits to the model to prevent feedback loops? What else can we think of that may harm others with these results?
